thread.title: Alphabet, Up 19% in 2018, Still Has Room to Rise

author: Andrew Bary
title: Alphabet, Up 19% in 2018, Still Has Room to Rise
text:
Google Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai (above, in 2015) said on the Alphabet conference call Monday that the video platform is “growing tremendously.” Illustration: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images By Andrew Bary July 24, 2018 5:59 p.m. ET Alphabet is showing that giants can still get bigger. The company logged a 26% gain in second-quarter revenues and better-than-expected earnings .
The company’s shares (ticker: GOOGL), which have lagged those of Amazon.com (AMZN) and Facebook (FB) so far this year, gained $47.15, or 3.9%, Tuesday to $1,258.15 after hitting a record high of $1,275 earlier in the day. The stock now is up 19% this year, behind Amazon’s 56% advance and Facebook’s 21% rise.
The shares still look reasonably priced at about 26 times estimated 2019 earnings of $48 a share—which includes the company’s significant stock-based compensation expense, now running at rate of more than $9 billion annually, or about $100,000 for each of the company’s 89,000 employees. Alphabet’s annual stock comp is running at about $10 a share. Many tech companies encourage investors to strip out that very real expense, but Alphabet doesn’t.
The earnings include more than $3 a share in annual losses from the company’s valuable “Other Bets” businesses like Waymo, the leading developer of autonomous driving technology. Alphabet also is sitting on $98 billion of net cash and equivalents, or nearly $140 per share. Adjust for the Other Bets losses and the cash, and the effective 2019 price/earnings ratio is closer to 22.
That’s still a premium to the S&P 500, which trades at about 16 times next year’s projected operating earnings. But analysts say the company is capable of generating mid- to high-teens annual earnings growth in the coming years—about double that of the S&P.
Newsletter Sign-up On Monday, Alphabet reported $11.75 in second-quarter earnings per share, about $2 above the consensus estimate, excluding a $5.07 billion European Commission fine for antitrust violations related to the company’s Android operating system. Alphabet is contesting that ruling. Factoring in the fine, Alphabet earned $4.54 a share. Revenue rose 26% in the period to $32.7 billion, topping estimates.
“There has been a change in the Alphabet story. Investors have gone from being skeptical about the growth in operating expenses and capital expenditures to endorsing them now that they’re bearing fruit with strong revenue growth,” says Anthony DiClemente, an Evercore ISI analyst who has an Outperform rating and a $1,350 price target on the stock.
Alphabet’s sales are expected to hit about $137 billion this year. There are few companies besides Amazon with over $100 billion in annual revenues that are growing so rapidly.
Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak wrote in a client note today that the company is “investing harder than ever to extend its advantage.” Alphabet spent $5.3 billion on capital expenditures in the period and $12.8 billion in the first six months of 2018. That compares with $13.2 billion for all of 2017. The 2018 capex includes $2.4 billion spent to purchase the Chelsea Market property in Manhattan.
But even excluding that real estate deal, Alphabet’s capex is running at an annual rate of more than $20 billion. Alphabet has one of the highest capex levels among American companies, topping Apple (AAPL), which spent $7 billion in the first six months of its fiscal year ending Sept. 30, and Amazon, which spent $12.9 billion during the 12 months ended March 31. Alphabet also is pouring money into research and development, spending $10.2 billion in the first six months of 2018.
Nowak today lifted his Alphabet price target to $1,325 from $1,250 while maintaining an Overweight rating.
The commercial potential of Alphabet businesses like YouTube and Waymo could drive Alphabet toward a $1 trillion market value, which would equate to a stock price of more than $1,400 a share, Nowak argues. He wrote recently that Waymo’s industry-leading technology in self-driving cars could lead to a “winner take most” position as the company is expected to roll out its first commercial service this year. He has estimated that Waymo could be worth $75 billion. Ride-sharing services are expected to be a key use of autonomous vehicle technology.
Alphabet doesn’t disclose revenues or profitability for either Waymo or YouTube. Investors are particularly interested in seeing the YouTube sales. Google Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai said on the Alphabet conference call Monday that the video platform is “growing tremendously.” DiClemente estimates that YouTube’s revenues this year will rise around 35% to $16 billion and increase another 25% next year to $20 billion. He values YouTube at $100 billion, while Nowak thinks it could be worth over $150 billion.
Many investors are wary of the FANG stocks (Facebook, Amazon, Netflix [NFLX], and Google parent Alphabet) given their gains and outsize contribution to the S&P 500’s advance this year. But DiClemente says that the four companies continue to “increase the barriers to entry” in their businesses. He estimates that combined capex of the four companies will total $60 billion next year, with an additional $70 billion spent on research and development.
Alphabet’s stock-buyback program, at about $2 billion per quarter, remains modest relative to its earnings power. That roughly offsets the stock issued to employees as compensation and has resulted in little change in the company’s share count, which ended the second quarter at 703 million, valuing the company at about $875 billion.
Barron’s has been bullish on Alphabet, including an article earlier this year ( “Google’s Parent Is a Bargain in Big Tech,” April 7, 2018), and has also argued that the company should become more aggressive with its buyback program.
Alphabet remains a strong growth story with a dominant position in search advertising and a series of valuable businesses including YouTube and Waymo that aren’t fully reflected in its stock price.
